title: A performance refactor of AdminPermission.projects split one combined Q filter into chained .filter(teams__members=user).filter(teams__access=ADMIN_ACCESS) calls, so read-only team members get admin rights on any project that also belongs to some admin team.

findings.explanation: This code uses Django ORM with parameterized queries. All user input is passed through Django's filter() and exclude() methods which use bound parameters. The 'user' object is a Django model instance, not raw SQL. The string literals 'teams__members', 'teams__access', 'organizations__ssointegration__provider', and SSOIntegration.PROVIDER_ALLAUTH are all application-controlled constants, not user input. No SQL injection vulnerability is present.

The refactored logic changes the authorization check semantics. The original code uses OR logic: if admin=True, include ADMIN_ACCESS teams; if member=True, include READ_ONLY_ACCESS teams. The new code uses exclusive conditions: 'if admin and not member' vs 'elif member and not admin'. When both admin and member are True, the new code skips all access-level filtering (just the 'pass' comment), potentially returning projects from both ADMIN_ACCESS and READ_ONLY_ACCESS teams. This could represent incorrect authorization logic depending on the intended behavior—if both flags being True should apply stricter filtering or specific logic, the change may violate authorization requirements. However, without seeing how admin/member parameters are set by callers, this is unconfirmed.
findings.suggested_fix: Clarify the intended authorization semantics when both admin and member are True. If the original OR logic should be preserved, replace the conditional block with: 'filter = Q(); if admin: filter |= Q(teams__access=ADMIN_ACCESS); if member: filter |= Q(teams__access=READ_ONLY_ACCESS); projects_from_teams = projects_from_teams.filter(filter)' to maintain the original behavior.
